Essentials 2.0 · Flow inspiration · 09-mobile-ipad

Mobile and iPad app: ideas from other products

This page shows phone and iPad examples from other products for running a live simulation without a desktop, grouped by product. They cover recording control, checklists, timers, learner tagging, dictated notes, intercom, the sim tech's room check, and private debrief notes. The focus is how the device behaves: live status, lock screen, one-hand use, large controls, and iPad layouts. Desktop and the session video review screen (SRV) are in 04-recording. The QR phone remote is in 08-debrief-review. Sources are the design reference libraries Mobbin and Refero. All flows shown are from Mobbin. Refero was searched, but its image server refused the downloads, so no Refero flow made the report. Researched on 30 September 2026.

What we have today. Today TouchPro is LearningSpace's only tablet client, and there is no phone app. The solution concept of 10 September 2026 proposes a QR-scan checklist and remote start and stop for recording. It also proposes private debrief notes, a sim-tech setup checklist, and a timer (customers buy separate digital timers today). It further proposes learner tagging, timestamped speech-to-text notes, and the phone as an intercom microphone. Constraints: a web page is preferred for the debrief page. Phones may be banned in graded exams. Tablets must not be required. No biometrics tied to names may go to the cloud. Leadership wants to see which jobs truly benefit from mobile before committing to a first version (MVP).

How to read this page

Each section below is one product. Each strip of screenshots is one flow: a real sequence of screens, in the order a user sees them. Click a screenshot to enlarge it. "Worth borrowing" lists ideas we could use, and "Avoid" lists what we should not copy. Use the task filters to see only one task, and click ☆ on a flow to add it to your own shortlist.

14 products · 22 flows · 113 screens · 8 tasks

What the best products have in common

  1. One unmistakable record status, and bookmark with the same thumb GoPro Quik shows remaining storage and battery before you start. It turns the record button into a stop square, keeps a red dot and elapsed time visible, and puts a 'HiLight' button next to stop with a full-screen 'tagged' confirmation. That pairs recording control with a one-tap timed marker, which is what faculty need while walking the room. Journal keeps the recording status alive on the lock screen. Neither shows which room or camera is being controlled, which Essentials must add.See: GoPro Quik: Recording a video · Journal: Live Activities
  2. The timer lives outside the app, but only in an installed phone app Forest puts remaining time, the phase name and a single stop control on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island (the status area at the top of newer iPhones). Toggl offers full-screen digits for reading across the room. This is the strongest evidence in the module that a job benefits from a phone rather than the SRV. It also only works in an installed phone app (a native app), so a web page or a phone-banned exam gets none of it. A large in-app full-screen timer is the fallback that must work everywhere.See: Forest: Live Activities · Forest: Dynamic Island · Toggl Track: Tracking time with Pomodoro technique
  3. Named phases, pause is not end, restart from history Toggl separates Stop (pause the clock) from End session (finish the cycle). It flips colour and label when the phase changes, and asks before skipping a phase. Its timer list lets you restart any named timer with one tap. Simulation phases (briefing, scenario, debrief) repeat every session. Restarting from history beats configuring a new countdown each time.See: Toggl Track: Tracking time with Pomodoro technique · Toggl Track: Timer
  4. Confirm the person, then stay ready for the next one Luma shows a confirmation panel (name, status, ticket) before checking someone in. It then returns straight to the scanner with a success message and offers Undo. Zoom admits people from a waiting-room message and keeps a participant count on the toolbar. Both treat who is in the session as a fast, reversible stream at the door, not a form with a list of people. That matches tagging learners on a phone.See: Luma: Checking in a guest (scan QR code) · Luma: Checking in guests · Zoom: Starting a new meeting
  5. Every note carries its time label Otter pins a time label to each comment and a speaker-plus-time stamp to each transcript paragraph. Fabric saves frame drawings as 'Drawing · 00:00:00' entries and keeps a time label on the reply field. Fabric's voice note diverges: its transcript has no per-line timestamps, so text cannot be traced back to a moment. None of the flows shows an on-device versus cloud transcription indicator.See: Otter AI: Adding a comment · Otter AI: Editing transcript · Fabric: Drawing on a video · Fabric: Creating a voice note
  6. Talking into a room is a mode, with live and muted always visible Slack makes push-to-talk (PTT) an explicit mode with a large hold button. It shows muted status on both your picture and the control. Alexa separates a live 'Drop In' from a one-way 'Announce' behind an opt-in. Zoom shows 'connecting to audio' before you can be heard. For a phone that talks into a live sim room, the risk is an open mic. Hold-to-talk plus a persistent live or muted status is the default to copy.See: Slack: Turning on push-to-talk · Amazon Alexa: Communication · Zoom: Starting a new meeting
  7. Name the screen you are driving; pairing must be one step Google TV's remote keeps a docked bar naming the connected screen and offers 30-second skip buttons. That suits jumping between debrief moments. Getting there takes five steps of Wi-Fi or Bluetooth discovery, which fails a faculty member in a debrief room. Keep the named-screen bar and simple playback buttons, but pair by QR as 08-debrief-review proposes.See: Google TV: Remote (movie) · Google TV: Connecting to a TV
  8. One big item at a time beats a checkbox list Lifesum fills a scored assessment one item per screen, with answer rows as wide as the screen. It keeps Next disabled until an answer is picked, uses a slider for graded answers, and ends with a score breakdown. Fabric's standard small checkboxes fail gloved, one-handed use. American Airlines groups readiness into one place with time-limited tasks but has no pass/fail statuses. The live checklist needs Lifesum's large answer rows and review step without its 41-item length.See: Lifesum: Completing a test (life score) · Fabric: Marking a checklist as done · American Airlines: Ready to fly

Questions we still need to answer

  • No iPad flows. Mobbin's search has no iPad filter and every shortlisted flow is a phone layout. The only tablet layout found, Superlist, is a generic list with a detail pane. The tablet-versus-phone question from stakeholders is not answered here. It needs a manual pass through Mobbin's iPad catalogue or an audit of TouchPro.
  • The strongest mobile wins (lock-screen timer, recording status on the lock screen (Live Activity), background push-to-talk) only work in an installed app. A web-first debrief page and phone bans in graded exams mean they cannot be the core of the MVP. Which jobs justify a native app, and does each have a web or tablet fallback?
  • Equipment check has no end-to-end reference. Nothing shows scanning a room QR, ticking items pass/fail, flagging a broken item and handing off. The flow has to be assembled from Luma's scan-and-confirm, Lifesum's large-target items, American Airlines' readiness place and Yuka's per-item problem report with a required photo.
  • No flow shows an on-device versus cloud transcription indicator. EU data-protection rules (GDPR) make that a requirement for speech-to-text notes. This has to be designed without a reference.
  • Live rubrics: Lifesum shows that 41 one-at-a-time items are too slow for a live scenario. How long are real objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) checklists? Do they need sections, a grid on tablet, or partial scoring after the session?
  • Learner tagging is covered for who is present (Luma, Zoom) but not for who did what. Only GoPro's HiLight shows tagging a moment, with no person attached. Refero was searched but its image server blocked the downloads, so no Refero flows could be included.

GoPro Quik

Same task, different field1 flow

GoPro Quik makes the phone a camera remote. It shows storage and battery before you start, turns the record button into stop, and puts a one-thumb 'HiLight' bookmark button beside stop.

iOSMobbin4 steps

Recording a video

From an idle remote view with camera status, the user starts recording and marks a moment with HiLight. A full-screen confirmation appears, then the live recording screen returns with elapsed timer and stop.

Recording control

Worth borrowing

  • While idle, a top strip shows remote camera storage remaining (3H:25), Wi-Fi and battery before start. You can check readiness without leaving the control screen.
  • While recording, the main control changes from a red record circle to a white-ring red-square stop, and an elapsed time label appears above the feed.
  • HiLight is a one-thumb yellow mark button beside stop. A short full-screen 'HiLIGHT TAGGED' confirms the bookmark without opening a list.
  • After the tag message closes, a red dot and elapsed timer keep recording status easy to see.

Avoid

  • The idle and recording view is a large black empty plane with tiny mode details (1080|24|10s|W). Faculty need a named room or camera and clear live-preview status, not cryptic capture specs.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: the phone wins as a walk-around remote start and stop for room cameras (extends TouchPro; no phone app today). HiLight maps to one-tap timed bookmarks during a live take. Keep a large stop and an unmistakable recording indicator.

Luma

Same task, different field2 flows

Luma handles QR check-in at the door. You confirm the person on a panel that slides up, get a short success message while the scanner stays open, and can undo a wrong check-in.

iOSMobbin3 steps

Checking in a guest (scan QR code)

The host opens Scan to Check In, confirms a scanned guest on a panel, then gets a green success message while the scanner stays ready for the next person.

Learner tagging

Worth borrowing

  • A confirm-before-commit guest panel with name, email and status before Check In (screen 2) prevents wrong roster tags.
  • A green success message without leaving the scanner (screen 3) keeps throughput for a line of learners.
  • A List or Scan control plus search shortcut (screen 1) gives a QR fail path without abandoning the flow.
  • A flashlight control on the scan chrome (screen 1) helps in poorly lit rooms.

Avoid

  • Do not tag this as equipment check. The screens only show guest ticket check-in, not room or device setup.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: mobile beats desktop for door-side learner tagging. QR scan plus one-tap confirm replaces paper roster or SRV search. The same pattern maps to room QR for equipment check, but this flow itself is people only.

iOSMobbin4 steps

Checking in guests

From an event card the host opens Check In, scans a guest, confirms identity, then can Undo Check In after success.

Learner tagging

Worth borrowing

  • Check In is a first-class action on the session or event card (screen 1), not buried in settings.
  • A confirm panel before commit (screen 3) shows name, status Going and ticket type.
  • Undo Check In on the success panel (screen 4) recovers fast from an accidental scan.
  • A flip-camera control on the scanner (screen 2) supports front or rear for badge versus phone-held QR.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: phone in hand at the room door beats TouchPro-only tagging. Extends baseline learner tagging and QR checklist with undo and confirm.

Otter AI

Close match2 flows

In Otter AI, every paragraph and every comment shows a speaker and a time. Playback stays above the keyboard while you correct the transcript.

iOSMobbin5 steps

Adding a comment

From transcript playback the user opens the plus tray, chooses Comment, composes a reply anchored to a timestamp label, and sees it land in a threaded view.

Debriefing tool: annotations

Worth borrowing

  • A timestamp pin label on the comment panel (screens 3 to 5) always shows which moment the note belongs to.
  • A plus tray grouping Comment with photo capture (screen 2) gives one entry for moment evidence.
  • A snippet of transcript above the compose field (screens 3 to 4) keeps context without leaving the thread.
  • A comment count next to the timestamp label after post (screen 5) shows the annotation stuck.

Avoid

  • Starting the add path from a small plus on the player (screen 2) is easy to miss for one-hand or gloved use. Prefer a larger Add comment target.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: mobile beats fixed SRV for private timestamped faculty notes during playback. Maps directly to baseline debrief annotations. Prefer a web page for shared big-screen control.

iOSMobbin4 steps

Editing transcript

From a timestamped transcript playback view the user enters edit mode, corrects a word inline with the keyboard while the scrubber stays available, then exits with the corrected selection visible.

Speech-to-text note takingDebriefing tool: annotations

Worth borrowing

  • A speaker block and start timestamp on every paragraph (screen 1) ties text to audio without a separate timeline.
  • A floating playback bar above the keyboard while editing (screens 2 to 3) lets you scrub or skip ±5s without leaving edit.
  • Explicit Done versus pencil header statuses (screens 2 to 4) make enter and exit for inline transcript correction clear.
  • Highlighter, comment and image actions on the player (screen 1) let the same moment be marked while correcting text.

Avoid

  • A dense metadata header (keywords, speakers, share) above the transcript (screen 1) competes with glanceable playback for gloved faculty.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: mobile wins for post-session transcript fix-ups beside the recording. Extends baseline timestamped speech-to-text notes and can feed private debrief moments. It is not a live-room control replacement.

Toggl Track

Same task, different field2 flows

Toggl Track has named phase timers with large full-screen digits. Stop pauses the clock and End session finishes it, and any past timer restarts with one tap.

iOSMobbin12 steps

Tracking time with Pomodoro technique

From the timer list, the user switches to Pomodoro, names and tags a focus session, and starts through notification prompts. They run including full-screen, reach near-end, then hit the break phase and confirm skipping it.

Timer

Worth borrowing

  • When ready, a session label and project or person label sit above a huge dial. Full-width Start session and an expand control open room-visible full-screen.
  • While running, Stop pauses the clock and underlined End focus session finishes the cycle. Those are two distinct end intents.
  • Full-screen uses oversized digits plus Stop and Exit full-screen for across-the-room readability.
  • Break flips colour and label (green Break / Relax!) and asks for confirmation before Skip this break.

Avoid

  • Back-to-back in-app then system notification permission dialogs mid-run interrupt the live session. Ask for permissions before start.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: mobile or a propped tablet beats the SRV for in-room phase timers customers buy separately today. Full-screen and phase colours replace dedicated digital timers. Pomodoro work and break labels would map to sim phases, not focus or break slang.

View on Mobbin ↗
iOSMobbin4 steps

Timer

From an empty timer list with a start tip, the list fills with today's entries and restart plays. Then come suggestions plus activity, then multi-day history with favorites and a sticky start bar.

Timer

Worth borrowing

  • When empty, an illustration and tip pinned to the thumb-zone play button teaches first start.
  • In the list, each past entry has a one-tap play to restart the same named timer.
  • Suggestions are hideable quick-restart cards above activity for frequent phases.
  • A sticky bottom bar with I'm working on and a large play stays available while scrolling history.

Avoid

  • The list alone does not show an active running status or room-visible countdown. Pair it with a dedicated running or fullscreen surface for live sim phases.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: mobile helps faculty and tech juggle multiple named phase timers on the floor (extends separate digital timers). Restart-from-history is the win over desktop for repeating scenario phases.

Forest

Same task, different field2 flows

Forest is the clearest case for a phone timer. Remaining time and phase show on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island, with one stop control, without opening the app.

iOSMobbin3 steps

Live Activities

A lock-screen Live Activity shows a Rest countdown with dismiss, then a Study countdown with a progress bar, then a completed-focus summary with restart and today's total.

Timer

Worth borrowing

  • During Rest, large remaining time, a phase label and one X control appear without unlocking.
  • During Study, the same chrome adds a thin progress bar under the phase label.
  • When done, the lock screen shows outcome text, a start-to-end clock range, a restart control and today's total.

Avoid

  • This depends on native Live Activities. That clashes with a preferred web debrief client and phone-ban exams. Treat it as a native-only pattern, not the primary MVP surface.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: only mobile can show phase time on the lock screen (desktop and SRV cannot). That is strong evidence the timer job benefits from a phone. Extend room timers with always-visible remaining time for faculty holding devices between tasks.

Dynamic Island

The Dynamic Island shows a compact sprout and countdown while the app is backgrounded, then expands to countdown, Rest phase label, and an X stop control.

Timer

Worth borrowing

  • Compact: remaining time stays in the system chrome while you work elsewhere in the OS.
  • Expanded: a phase label under the time plus a single X ends the timer without opening the app.

Avoid

  • iPhone Dynamic Island only is useless on generic tablets or web and during phone-banned graded exams. Do not require it.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: this shows why mobile (not the SRV) can keep a session timer glanceable during other work. Prefer a lock-screen or widget-like always-on timer where the OS allows, with a large in-app fallback for web and tablet.

Slack

Same task, different field1 flow

Slack makes push-to-talk a mode you switch on. It uses a large button you hold to speak and shows muted status in two places.

iOSMobbin4 steps

Turning on push-to-talk

In an active huddle the user opens More, turns on push-to-talk, then gets a large hold-to-speak microphone control with clear muted versus live cues.

Intercom device

Worth borrowing

  • Push-to-talk is a mode you switch on under More (screen 1), so open mic versus hold-to-talk is a decision, not assumed.
  • A full-width muted push-to-talk screen with an X to leave (screen 2) shows you are not live before speaking.
  • An oversized bottom microphone button (screens 3 to 4) lets faculty who are gloved or holding gear hold to talk with one thumb.
  • A mute badge on the You tile plus the bottom control (screens 2 to 4) shows live or muted in two places.

Avoid

  • Burying push-to-talk only under More (screen 1) is wrong for a dedicated room intercom; the mode should not require hunting in overflow.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: the phone wins as an intercom microphone. Hold-to-talk with a large button reduces open-mic risk into a live sim room. This extends the baseline intercom, not the SRV.

Amazon Alexa

Same task, different field1 flow

Alexa separates a live two-way 'Drop In' from a one-way 'Announce', and Drop In has to be allowed explicitly. Most tools merge these two kinds of intercom.

iOSMobbin3 steps

Communication

From the More screen the user opens Communicate, is asked to enable Household Drop In as an intercom, then lands on Communication with separate Drop In and Announce targets.

Intercom device

Worth borrowing

  • 'Drop In' and 'Announce' are separate top actions (screen 3), so live room intercom and one-way broadcast are not the same control.
  • An Enable prompt with 'Later' and 'Enable' asks for opt-in before the phone can drop into rooms or devices (screen 2).
  • The prompt promises 'See recently active devices' (screen 2), so you can see which rooms are alive before connecting.
  • A large Communicate tile sits among peer jobs on More (screen 1), so gloved or one-hand use is easier.

Avoid

  • A promo banner on the Communication screen (screen 3) competes with the Drop In and Announce targets.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: the phone beats the SRV as an intercom into a sim room. Separate Drop In (live) versus Announce (broadcast) would extend the baseline intercom mic idea. This is not a desktop-only job.

Google TV

Same task, different field2 flows

Google TV drives a big screen from the phone. A bar at the bottom names the connected screen and has 30-second skip buttons. Its five-step Wi-Fi pairing is an example of what not to do compared with pairing by QR code.

iOSMobbin2 steps

Remote (movie)

While browsing a title with Living Room TV already connected, the user opens the full remote and gets touchpad nav plus play/pause, seek, and ±30s skips for the big screen.

Debriefing tool: annotations

Worth borrowing

  • A docked bar naming Living Room TV with pause while browsing (screen 1) lets you control without leaving context.
  • A Connected header on the remote panel (screen 2) always shows which screen is driven.
  • ±30s skips beside the scrubber (screen 2) support coarse jumps for debrief moments without precise scrubbing.
  • Large mute and volume targets under the touchpad (screen 2) are one-hand, glanceable audio and video controls.

Avoid

  • A full swipe-to-navigate touchpad as primary (screen 2) is wrong for debrief. Debrief needs timeline and bookmarks, not TV focus navigation.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: the phone beats desktop for faculty standing in the room driving the debrief big screen. Prefer a web remote with named screen and transport or skip after QR pair. That extends baseline private annotations and screen control.

iOSMobbin5 stepsExample of what not to do

Connecting to a TV

From For you the user taps TV Nearby and picks Living Room TV from a Wi-Fi or Bluetooth discovery list. They confirm selection, see Turning on, then a persistent Connected bar with a remote shortcut.

Debriefing tool: annotations

Worth borrowing

  • Named devices under AVAILABLE DEVICES (screen 2) show room or screen identity before control.
  • A green check on the selected TV (screen 3) confirms which screen before committing.
  • A Turning on message then Connected with the named TV (screens 4 to 5) gives power and link feedback.
  • A persistent Connected bar with a remote shortcut (screen 5) keeps you in context while linked to the big screen.

Avoid

  • Five-step same-network Wi-Fi or Bluetooth discovery (screens 1 to 5) is slow and brittle compared with a QR on the debrief display for faculty pairing.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: this is an example of what not to do for debrief pairing. Multi-step nearby discovery does not beat a QR-linked web page on the phone. Keep named-screen and Connected chrome if pairing is QR-first.

Lifesum

Outside idea1 flow

Lifesum fills in a scored assessment one item at a time, with full-width answer rows, a slider for graded answers and a score breakdown at the end. It also shows how slow 41 items are.

iOSMobbin11 steps

Completing a test (life score)

The user starts a Life Score test from 0/150, answers radio and multi-select items plus a frequency slider, then reviews a scored Weekly insights breakdown with retake.

Checklist interface

Worth borrowing

  • NEXT stays disabled until a choice is made (screens 2 and 4), so rubric items must be completed.
  • Large full-row radio and multi-check targets (screens 2 to 5) suit one-hand, gloved scoring.
  • A continuous slider with a live value label for graded items (screens 6 to 7) is a partial-credit analog.
  • After submit, a score gauge and grouped status cards from OPTIMAL to OFF-TRACK (screens 8 to 11) support review after fill.

Avoid

  • A 41-step path for live scoring is too slow during a sim (screen 6). Keep rubrics short or sectioned.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: one question at a time beats desktop forms for faculty filling a rubric live. Extends baseline checklist with large targets and a scored summary. Compress length for exam constraints.

Zoom

Same task, different field1 flow

Zoom admits people from a waiting-room message, shows a participant count on the toolbar, and says clearly that it is connecting to audio before you can be heard. It shows no recording control.

iOSMobbin9 steps

Starting a new meeting

The host starts a meeting from the phone, grants mic access, admits a waiting-room participant, then runs the live session with mute and a participant count.

Learner taggingIntercom device

Worth borrowing

  • A waiting-room message with primary Admit and secondary View (screen 5) lets you admit who enters without opening a full roster.
  • A Participants count on the toolbar (screens 4, 8 and 9) shows who is in the session at a glance.
  • Clear Mute versus muted-slash status on the toolbar and on the remote tile (screens 4, 7 and 8) models live versus muted for intercom.

Fabric

Same task, different field3 flows

Fabric saves drawings on a video frame as timed comments, and has a large Stop/Resume voice note with transcript tabs, but no sign of whether transcription ran on the device. Its tiny checkbox list is an example of what not to do.

Drawing on a video

From a paused video the user opens draw tools, marks a person with a freehand circle, saves the drawing, then sees it as a timestamped Drawing entry in Comments.

Worth borrowing

  • Vertical tool rail icons stay relatively small on the frame (screens 2 to 4). That is risky for gloved faculty; enlarge primary pen and save.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: mobile is strong for private frame markup during debrief walk-around. Extends baseline debrief annotations. Keep big-screen control on web or SRV; phone or tablet for personal draws.

Creating a voice note

Same task, different field2 flows

Journal shows recording status on the lock screen with a waveform, a timer and one stop control, but no pause. In the app, 'Done' stays disabled until you pause.

iOSMobbin2 steps

Live Activities

From the lock screen, the user monitors an in-progress audio recording Live Activity (waveform and elapsed time) and ends it with a single stop or done control, without unlocking.

Recording control

Worth borrowing

  • Recording status is glanceable without unlocking: a live waveform and elapsed timer on the lock screen (both screens).
  • A single primary end-recording control on the Live Activity (stop square then checkmark) has no secondary chrome (screens 1 to 2).
  • The control stays large beside the waveform so one-handed stop works while pocketed or gloved (screen 1).

  • There is no pause on the Live Activity (both screens), only stop or done. A pocket tap can discard mid-thought with no resume.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: only a phone can control recording from the lock screen. Recording an audio

Speech-to-text note takingRecording control

Worth borrowing

  • Record starts as a bottom panel over the note so context stays visible (screen 2).
  • When paused, Done is enabled and you can scrub or play the take before committing (screen 5).
  • Done stays disabled until pause or stop so you cannot finalize mid-record (screens 3 to 4).
  • A finished take collapses to a compact player card on the note (screen 6).

Avoid

  • A quote or transcript icon appears on the recorder and card (screens 3 to 6) but no transcript screen is shown. Do not imply speech-to-text from these screens alone.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: phone-side dictate-and-attach for baseline timestamped voice notes while walking the room. Extends TouchPro with pause and scrub-before-save. This is not room audio and video start or stop.

American Airlines gathers readiness for one event in one place, with tasks that open at set times (what you can do now and what not yet). It has no pass, fail or flag statuses.

iOSMobbin4 steps

Ready to fly

A traveler opens a trip overview, enters Get ready to fly, then scrolls a Ready to Fly set of time-limited prep tasks and know-before-you-go items.

Equipment checkChecklist interface

Worth borrowing

  • A single Ready to Fly place keyed to one event or trip (screens 3 to 4) keeps pre-session readiness in one place.
  • Cards show time remaining or not-yet-available wording (screen 3), so you see what cannot be done yet versus what to do now.
  • Missing-data placeholders (--) on the trip card (screen 1) make incomplete setup fields easy to spot.
  • An entry panel from the trip (screen 2) nudges into the checklist without hunting menus.

Avoid

  • Informational cards without tick, flag or broken statuses (screens 3 to 4) leave sim-tech equipment check without clear pass or fail.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: a mobile readiness place fits walking the floor before a session better than desktop. Extend baseline equipment check and checklist with time-limited tasks, but add real tick and flag handoff that American Airlines lacks.

Yuka

Outside idea1 flow

Yuka lets you report a problem with an item you just scanned. You pick a category and attach a required photo ('Send' stays disabled without it), then get a thank-you with a response time.

iOSMobbin8 steps

Sending feedback

From Help, the user picks a recently scanned product, chooses an issue category, and selects which fields are wrong. They write a note, attach a required photo, and get a thank-you with a 48-hour follow-up.

Equipment check

Worth borrowing

  • Recent scans act as reporting shortcuts with a thumb and relative time (screen 1), so you jump to the item you just touched.
  • The scanned-item header (photo, name, status, age) stays while picking issue type (screens 2 and 8).
  • A required-photo label and disabled Send until evidence is attached (screens 5 to 7) force proof before submit.
  • A camera versus library sheet puts Take a picture first (screen 7). A closed-loop Thank you plus reply-within time closes the loop (screen 8).

Avoid

  • A deep multi-step path (issue, field pick, note, photo) is too many screens for a gloved sim tech flagging missing or broken gear on a pre-session walk.

What it means for Essentials Mobile and iPad app: this fits equipment check as an analog. It starts from a scanned item with issue categories and a required photo. It is not a room QR checklist or tick-all walkthrough. Mobile beats the SRV because the tech is at the broken gear. Extend baseline sim-tech setup with item-level flag and evidence handoff.
